## Yield Histories, Distance, and Causal Reach

A translation-yield cosmology has three distinct levels. The endpoint ratio compares a signal at emission and observation. The intervening history determines how much translation accumulates along the path. Geometry and transport then determine which observable distance is inferred from that propagation.

The local descriptor of a yield history is

$$
H_\chi(t)=-\frac{\dot\chi(t)}{\chi(t)}.
$$

If $\chi$ decreases forward in time, $H_\chi$ is positive. Under the formal correspondence $\chi\propto1/a$, it takes the same algebraic form as the usual expansion rate,

$$
H_\chi=\frac{\dot a}{a}.
$$

That correspondence does not make $H_\chi$ a complete observational Hubble function. It identifies the local fractional rate associated with a chosen translation-yield history.

The endpoint ratio

$$
1+z=\frac{\chi_e}{\chi_o}
$$

does not specify the path between its endpoints. Two histories can produce the same redshift while assigning different emission times, propagation intervals, lookback durations, and rates of change along the way.

The second level is the history kernel already established for lightlike translation,

$$
\mathcal D_\chi(t_e,t_o)
=
c\int_{t_e}^{t_o}\chi(t)\,dt.
$$

The endpoint ratio answers how an emitted interval is compared with an observed interval. The integral answers how much background translation accumulates between the two events. A value of $z$ therefore does not by itself fix $t_e$, the elapsed interval $t_o-t_e$, or $\mathcal D_\chi$. Those depend on the chosen history and on whatever dynamics determine it.

The third level is an observable distance. Radial propagation, angular size, flux dilution, and lookback time are different measurements. Turning $\mathcal D_\chi$ into any one of them requires source–observer geometry, angular relations, area transport, local clock and ruler conventions, and a definition of the distance being inferred.

The history kernel also controls causal reach at the kinematic level. If earlier values of $\chi$ were larger, lightlike influence would accumulate more displacement per unit of the background time parameter than a constant-yield extrapolation would suggest:

$$
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{causal}}
\sim
c\int\chi(t)\,dt.
$$

That possibility can change how age, horizon, or early-structure questions are posed. It does not settle them. Recombination, cooling, binding, perturbation growth, collapse, mergers, and source populations all require their own dynamics.

The boundary is now clean. Translation yield supplies the kinematic engine. The endpoint dictionary supplies linked wavelength and duration mappings. A proposed history $\chi(t)$ supplies rates and propagation kernels. Only after those pieces are combined with geometry, matter, and signal transport does the construction become an observational cosmology.
